title: Taipei Faces a 'Double Ageing' Problem: Older People in Older Homes
summaryZh: 台北長者比例全台最高，七成多住宅屋齡逾30年。
summaryHi: ताइपे में बुज़ुर्गों का अनुपात सबसे ज़्यादा, 74% घर 30 साल से पुराने।
summaryEs: Taipéi tiene la población más envejecida de Taiwán y viviendas cada vez más viejas.
summaryJa: 台北は高齢者比率が全国最高、住宅の7割超が築30年以上。
summaryKo: 타이베이, 고령 인구 비율 전국 최고…주택 74%가 30년 넘어.
summaryEn: Taipei has Taiwan's oldest population, and almost three in four of its homes are over 30 years old.
paragraphs: Taipei is grappling with a "double ageing" crisis, as both its population and its housing stock grow steadily older, according to government figures reported on Saturday.

In August, 24.76 percent of the capital's residents were 65 or older, the highest proportion among Taiwan's 22 administrative regions. Meanwhile, 74.47 percent of Taipei's homes were over 30 years old in the second quarter, the second-highest share nationwide. Seventeen regions have now reached "super-aged" status, meaning at least one in five people is a senior.

Analysts say the problem is partly historical. Taipei developed earlier than most of Taiwan, so many long-time residents still live in ageing walk-up blocks. Government subsidies for installing lifts have helped, but some buildings simply lack the space. Redevelopment is also slow, because undeveloped land is scarce and new supply cannot keep pace.

Housing costs add to the imbalance. Resale flats average about NT$800,000 per ping, and new projects often exceed NT$1 million, pushing younger buyers to Keelung, New Taipei and Taoyuan, from where they commute.

Huang Shu-wei of Colliers International Taiwan argued that policy should prioritise safety rather than redevelopment alone, suggesting tools such as reverse mortgages and senior-care trusts to turn home equity into income for older residents.
Taipei has a big problem. Many people in the city are old, and many homes are old too.
In August, about one in four people in Taipei was 65 or older. This is the highest number in Taiwan. Also, 74 percent of homes in Taipei are more than 30 years old.
Some old buildings have no lift. It is hard for old people to walk up many stairs every day. The government gives money to help buildings add a lift, but some buildings do not have space for one.
Homes in Taipei are very expensive, so many young people buy homes in New Taipei, Keelung or Taoyuan. They take the train to work. Experts say the city needs new ideas to keep everyone safe at home.
Taipei is facing what experts call a "double ageing" problem: its people are getting older, and so are its buildings.

Government data show that in August, 24.76 percent of Taipei residents were aged 65 or over, the highest share among Taiwan's 22 cities and counties. In the second quarter of the year, 74.47 percent of homes in the capital were more than 30 years old, the second-highest share in the country. Across Taiwan, the average home is now about 34 years old.

Many older residents live in walk-up apartments without lifts. The government has helped pay for lifts to be added, but not every building has enough room. An expert from Sinyi Realty said more help is needed for these families.

At the same time, high prices keep younger buyers away. A second-hand flat in Taipei costs about NT$800,000 per ping, so many young families move to New Taipei, Keelung or Taoyuan and travel to work by train.
Experts say Taipei should focus on making old homes safe, not just on rebuilding them.

Taipei is confronting what property analysts describe as a "double ageing" crisis: a population that is rapidly greying, living in a housing stock that is deteriorating alongside it.

Official data show that 24.76 percent of the capital's residents were 65 or older in August, the highest proportion of any of Taiwan's 22 administrative regions. In the second quarter, 74.47 percent of its homes were more than three decades old, second only to one other region. Nationally, the average dwelling is now 34.46 years old, and 17 regions have crossed the "super-aged" threshold of 20 percent seniors.

The roots of the problem are partly historical. Because Taipei urbanised earlier than the rest of the country, many elderly residents remain in walk-up apartments built decades ago. Subsidies for retrofitting lifts have made a difference, yet many buildings lack the physical space, and with undeveloped land scarce, the cycle of urban renewal has nearly stalled.
Soaring prices compound the imbalance. With resale flats averaging around NT$800,000 per ping, younger households are increasingly priced out and commute from Keelung, New Taipei or Taoyuan instead.

Huang Shu-wei of Colliers International Taiwan called the demographic shift "irreversible" and urged officials to put residents' safety ahead of redevelopment targets, combining reverse mortgages, senior-care trusts and insurance so that older owners can draw income from their homes.
Taipei is experiencing what analysts have termed a "double ageing" phenomenon, whereby an increasingly elderly population inhabits a housing stock that is itself approaching obsolescence.

The statistics are striking. As of August, 24.76 percent of the capital's residents were aged 65 or above, the highest proportion among Taiwan's 22 administrative regions, while 74.47 percent of its dwellings had exceeded 30 years of age by the second quarter. Across the country, the average home is now over 34 years old, and 17 regions qualify as "super-aged" societies.

Several factors underpin this situation. Taipei urbanised earlier than other areas, leaving many long-standing residents in walk-up apartments that predate modern accessibility standards. Although subsidies for installing lifts have been beneficial, numerous buildings lack sufficient space, and the scarcity of undeveloped land has caused urban renewal to stagnate.

Affordability compounds the problem. Resale apartments average roughly NT$800,000 per ping, effectively excluding younger buyers, who increasingly settle in Keelung, New Taipei or Taoyuan and commute.

Huang Shu-wei of Colliers International Taiwan characterised the demographic trend as "irreversible" and maintained that policymakers should prioritise safety over redevelopment quotas. He advocated integrating reverse mortgages, senior-care trusts and insurance products, enabling elderly homeowners to convert property equity into a sustainable income.
